To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) among patients who had recently used alcohol or any other drug, those who used cocaine, other drugs of the same class as cocaine (stimulants), or heroin had significantly lower adherence to ART compared to those who did not, and (2) the significant associations of cocaine and other stimulants with adherence suggest that they are important substances to address with interventions that target adherence to antiretrovials

In bivariate analyses, recent cocaine use, recent use of other stimulants (including methamphetamine and amphetamine), and recent heroin use were each independently associated with lower antiretrovinal adherence during the previous 4 weeks, but recent use of cannabis and alcohol was not associated with lower adherence.

the associations between recent substance use and adherence were stronger for cocaine, other stimulant and heroin use than for alcohol and cannabis use, and that these associations remained after controlling for sociodemographic characteristics, amount of alcohol consumption and recent use of alcohol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between substance use and adherence.
the development of interventions that can be used by clinicians to increase adherence to antiretrovials.
the development of interventions that improve antiretrovirus (ARV) adherence among HIV-infected patients, and we have developed several such interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence supports the conclusion that the use of cannabis, cocaine, and heroin is associated with non-adherence.

(1) there is an association between substance use and adherence to HIV medication; (2) the association is stronger for stimulant use than for alcohol use; (3) the association is strongest for recent cocaine use, followed by recent use of heroin and then recent use of other stimulants; (4) the association is weaker for recent alcohol use than for recent use of other substances; (5) the association is not stronger for recent use of cannabis than for recent use alcohol; and
the association of substance abuse with non-adherence is complex and not easily explained by a single factor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are significant associations between substance use and antiretrovirals.
the use of cocaine, other drugs, and alcohol were all negatively associated with antiretrovial adherence.
we are working to understand the role of substance use in HIV prevention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
substance use, particularly stimulants and opiates, is associated with poor adherence and may be important to target for intervention to improve adherence.
substance abuse is associated with non-adherence to antiretrovial medications.
substance abuse is a major barrier to antiretrovial adherence.
